1338.title: Salve Regina
1338.howItsDone: Catholics sing or say the Salve Regina at the end of Night Prayer in Ordinary Time, and it is also prayed at the end of the rosary; some religious communities sing it together in chant before the night's silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Regina Caeli: the Easter prayer, he is risen, as he said. Your line was queen of heaven, rejoice.

A valley of tears. A strange address to put in a prayer, and an honest one. After Easter and Pentecost, the Church settles into the long green stretch of the year it calls Ordinary Time. Just Mondays, laundry, work, a sick parent, a good dinner, a bad night. For that stretch, the song at the end of night prayer is the one that knows exactly where people live. It opens with a greeting, hail, holy queen, and before it's done it has named exile, sighing, mourning and weeping. You first met it on day one hundred twenty-three. Today, it goes slowly.
screen: `A VALLEY OF TEARS.` → `THE LONG GREEN STRETCH: ORDINARY TIME.` → `A SONG FOR ORDINARY DAYS.`

segments.voice: It moves in four steps. First, names: Salve Regina, mater misericordiae. Hail, queen, mother of mercy, our life, our sweetness and our hope. Second, the truth about where the singers stand. To you we cry, exiled children of Eve; to you we send up our sighs, mourning and weeping in this valley of tears. A few days ago Mary was the new Eve, who untied the knot. Here the singers call themselves Eve's children, still far from home. The prayer doesn't pretend that ordinary life is easy. It names the tears and keeps singing. Third, the request. Turn your eyes of mercy toward us, it asks, and after this exile, show us Jesus, the blessed fruit of your womb. That phrase comes from Elizabeth's greeting in Luke's Gospel, which the Douay-Rheims gives as "blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Notice what the prayer asks: not for Mary to stand in for her son, but to show him. The whole song leans toward him. Fourth, three last cries: O clemens, O pia, O dulcis Virgo Maria. O clement, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary. A story links those last cries to Saint Bernard of Clairvaux; it isn't certain. Either way, the song ends not with an argument but with a sigh of affection, on an ordinary night, in an ordinary valley, with the lights about to go out.

segments.voice: Name honestly one thing in your valley right now, then one sweetness that's also true, a person, a small joy, a reason for hope, and hold the two side by side, the way the prayer does. If you pray, say or sing the Salve Regina, from hail, holy queen to O sweet Virgin Mary; if you don't, name the same two again, one tear, one hope. If the valley ever feels too dark to bear, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

1339.title: The Memorare
1339.hook: remember, O most gracious Virgin, that never was it known
1339.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Memorare on their own, in hard moments and as a regular devotion, and some pray it in a short run of repetitions when they bring an urgent need to Mary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Salve Regina: the night song of ordinary days, honest about the valley of tears. Your line was hail, holy queen.

Never. Asking for something usually comes wrapped in hedges. Sorry to bother you. No pressure. Only if you have time. Here's a prayer that does the opposite. It doesn't open by asking; it opens by reminding. Remember, O most gracious Virgin Mary, it begins, that never was it known that anyone who fled to your protection, asked for your help, or sought your prayers, was left without help. That's a bold thing to say out loud, especially when you're the one in need. It sounds less like a petition than a child tugging a sleeve: you always come.
screen: `MOST ASKING COMES WITH HEDGES.` → `THIS PRAYER BEGINS BY REMINDING.` → `NEVER WAS IT KNOWN.`

segments.voice: Memorare is Latin for remember, and it names the prayer. The one praying asks Mary to remember her own record, the way you'd speak to a friend who has always come through: you know what you're like. The prayer stands on memory. Then the bold line, never was it known. It isn't a survey or a statistic. It's a statement of trust, the kind people make about those they love: in the stories handed down, she didn't turn anyone away. Where does that trust come from? Some Catholics point to a wedding at Cana. In John's Gospel, the wine runs out, and Mary notices and tells her son. In the Douay-Rheims: "They have no wine." Then she turns to the servants: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." She sees a need and brings it to Jesus. The Memorare asks her to do that again. Then the posture. Inspired with this confidence, it goes on, I fly to you, and before you I stand, sinful and sorrowful. Confidence and humility in one breath: I know you'll help, and I know I don't deserve it. It ends by asking the mother of the Word made flesh not to despise these words, but to hear and answer. Who wrote it? Tradition credits Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, and others trace its spread to a later French priest, also named Bernard. Nobody needs to settle that to pray it. The prayer itself only asks you to remember.

segments.voice: Bring one need to mind, the one you'd hedge about if you were asking a person, and name it plainly, without the sorry-to-bother-you. If you pray, pray the Memorare once, slowly, from remember, O most gracious Virgin Mary, to hear and answer me, and set your need inside it like a note in an envelope. If you don't, remember one time someone noticed what you needed before you asked, and came.

1340.title: The oldest Marian prayer
1340.hook: Sub tuum praesidium, found on an ancient papyrus: we fly to thy protection
1340.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Sub tuum praesidium in Latin or English, sometimes at the end of the rosary or of Night Prayer, and Eastern Christians sing it in their own languages at evening services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Memorare: a prayer that opens by reminding. Your line was never was it known.

A scrap of papyrus, written in Greek, torn at the edges, with only parts of its lines left. Someone wrote a few words of prayer on it, and when scholars pieced them together, they matched a prayer the Church still says. In Latin it begins Sub tuum praesidium; in the traditional English, we fly to thy protection, O holy Mother of God. No grand liturgy around it. No author's name. Just a handful of people, it seems, in some kind of trouble, running toward a mother.
screen: `A SCRAP OF PAPYRUS, IN GREEK.` → `SUB TUUM PRAESIDIUM.` → `PEOPLE RUNNING TOWARD A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: First, the nickname, and its question mark. People call this the oldest Marian prayer. Scholars argue about how old the papyrus is, and the argument isn't settled, so it's fair to hold the nickname loosely. What nobody needs to argue about is what the prayer says. Second, the picture. We fly to thy protection: fly here means flee, run for cover. It's the posture of the psalm about God's shelter, which in the Douay-Rheims says, "under his wings thou shalt trust." The prayer doesn't stand up straight and make a speech. It ducks under cover. Third, the name it calls her: Holy Mother of God, the first of the four teachings that opened this stretch on Mary. Here it isn't an argument in a council or a line in a creed. It's what people shout when they're running. Fourth, the word we. The prayer never says I. Despise not our petitions in our necessities, it goes on, but deliver us always from all dangers, O glorious and blessed Virgin. A group of people with real needs and real dangers, praying together. And it's still said: in Latin in the West, and in Greek and other languages in Eastern churches, at evening prayer and at the end of the rosary. Short enough for one breath. Old enough that its own age is a question. And plural, so whoever says it today says it with everyone who ever ran for the same shelter.

1341.title: The Akathist
1341.hook: a Byzantine hymn to Mary sung standing
1341.howItsDone: Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Christians sing the Akathist to the Mother of God standing, especially in Lent, and some pray it at home or in shorter parts through the week.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the oldest Marian prayer, the Sub tuum praesidium: people running for cover together. Your line was we fly to thee.

Here's a hymn whose name is an instruction about chairs. In the Byzantine churches, the Orthodox and the Eastern Catholic churches, there's a long hymn to Mary that nobody sits down for. Its name, the Akathist, means not sitting. The church fills, the singing starts, and the people stay on their feet, stanza after stanza, while one greeting comes around again and again: rejoice. A story people tell says it was once sung through a whole night, standing, by a city giving thanks for being saved from a siege. Whatever its history, the posture stuck.
screen: `A HYMN NAMED FOR NOT SITTING.` → `THE PEOPLE STAY ON THEIR FEET.` → `REJOICE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Akathistos, in Greek, means not seated. Standing is what a person does when someone they honor walks into the room, and the hymn makes that a whole service: the body says what the words are saying. Some people stand to show respect; some stand because they can't sit still with joy. This hymn asks for both. Then the greeting. The word that keeps returning is chaire, rejoice, or hail. It's the angel's word. In Luke's Gospel, Gabriel opens with it, which the Douay-Rheims renders "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee." The Akathist multiplies that one greeting, line after line, each rejoice hung with a new picture of Mary, the way the Litany of Loreto stacks its names. At the end of each long stanza comes the refrain: rejoice, unwedded bride. Then the story underneath. The hymn doesn't only praise; it walks through the Gospel. Gabriel's visit. The birth. The shepherds. The magi following the star. The rejoices rise out of the story, like applause at each turn of a play. Last, where it lives. Eastern churches sing it especially in Lent, and that includes the Byzantine Catholic churches, in full communion with Rome. For a Latin Catholic, it's a reminder that the Church breathes, in a phrase Pope John Paul the Second used, with two lungs, East and West. The same Mary, the same angel's word, said in a different key, and on your feet.

segments.voice: If you're able, stand up now; if you can't, sit up tall and let that be your standing, feet steady, shoulders loose, the way you'd straighten if someone had just walked in. If you pray, say the angel's greeting, hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee, or the refrain, rejoice, unwedded bride, once with each slow breath. If you don't, simply stand in honor of someone you love, and let your body say it.

1342.title: Częstochowa
1342.hook: Poland's Black Madonna, an icon with scars on her cheek
1342.howItsDone: Catholics venerate the icon of Our Lady of Częstochowa at the Jasna Góra monastery in Poland, where pilgrims come to pray before it, some walking there on foot, and copies of the icon hang in Polish churches and homes elsewhere.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Akathist: a long hymn to Mary that the Byzantine churches sing on their feet. Your line was sung standing.

Two thin cuts run down a woman's right cheek, and a third crosses them, like a scar that healed badly. They're on a painting: a dark icon of Mary holding her child, kept in a monastery on a hill in the Polish city of Częstochowa. Her face is solemn and dark brown, almost black, which is why people call her the Black Madonna. Her son sits on her arm, one hand raised. A precious image, and nobody has made it look new. Why would anyone keep the wound?
screen: `TWO CUTS ON A PAINTED CHEEK.` → `THE BLACK MADONNA.` → `WHY KEEP THE WOUND?`

segments.voice: Start with the stories. Tradition says Saint Luke painted it, on a tabletop from the house in Nazareth. Art historians argue about when and where it was really made, and Catholics are free to hold the legend lightly; it's a story people tell, not something the Church asks anyone to believe. Then the scars. Tradition says raiders once broke into the monastery and tried to carry the icon off, and when it wouldn't go, one of them struck her face with a sword. The image was repaired, but the cuts were left, or came back, depending on who tells it. And the dark color? Smoke from candles, age, the paint itself; people still debate it. Next, the country. Tradition says that when the monastery held out against an invading army, Poland's king named Mary queen of Poland. Through wars and hard years after, Poles kept coming to this hill, and pilgrims still walk there on foot, singing as they go. Last, the scars again. In the Book of Lamentations, a ruined city speaks to everyone who walks past her. In the Douay-Rheims: "O all ye that pass by the way, attend, and see if there be any sorrow like to my sorrow." Some readers have heard Mary in that voice. A pilgrim before this icon does what the verse asks: stops, and looks at the wound. The cut isn't damage to be hidden. For pilgrims from a country that knew invasion, she could be a mother who had been hurt too, and stayed.

1343.title: Apparitions and private revelation (CCC 67)
1343.hook: no apparition is required belief, even approved ones
1343.howItsDone: The Catholic Church distinguishes public revelation, completed in Christ, from private revelations such as approved apparitions; Catholics may honor approved apparitions and visit their shrines, but are not required to believe in them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Częstochowa: a Black Madonna with sword cuts on her cheek, and a legend about Saint Luke that Catholics may hold lightly. Your line was the scarred icon.

A woman at a parish fish fry says, between bites, that she's never been sure about Lourdes. The man across from her nearly drops his fork. Doesn't the Church approve it? Isn't that part of being Catholic? The next days make it urgent: a grotto in France, a field in Portugal, a church wall in Ireland, a school in Rwanda, a forest in Vietnam, all places where people say Mary appeared. First, the rule the Church uses for all of them. It's short, it's in the Catechism, and it may surprise the man with the fork.
screen: `NEVER SURE ABOUT LOURDES.` → `PLACES WHERE PEOPLE SAY MARY APPEARED.` → `FIRST, THE RULE.`

segments.voice: Begin with public revelation. The Letter to the Hebrews says God spoke in many ways through the prophets, and then, in the Douay-Rheims, "last of all, in these days hath spoken to us by his Son." The Catechism draws the conclusion: in Christ, God has said everything, and no new public revelation is to be expected before Christ comes again. That's the faith the whole Church holds and hands on. Then paragraph sixty-seven, and the other kind. Over the centuries, it says, there have been so-called private revelations, some recognized by the Church's authority. Private doesn't mean secret; a crowd might see it. It means they don't belong to the deposit of faith. Their job isn't to improve or complete Christ's revelation, but to help people live by it more fully in a particular time. Next, what approval means. When the Church approves a reported apparition, it's saying, in effect: nothing here contradicts the faith, and you may honor it. It isn't saying every Catholic is bound to believe it happened. The woman at the fish fry is free to stay unsure. The man is free to make a pilgrimage. Neither is a better Catholic for it. Last, the attitude. Paul gives one to an early church: "Despise not prophecies. But prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Not scorn, and not swallowing everything: testing, and keeping what's good.

1344.title: The tilma of Guadalupe
1344.hook: the image shows a pregnant Indigenous woman standing before the sun
1344.howItsDone: Catholics venerate the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe on Juan Diego's tilma, which hangs in the Basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City; pilgrims come to look at it and pray, and copies of the image hang in churches and homes across the Americas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, private revelation: visions can help people live the Gospel, but they never add to it. Your line was never required.

Her hands are pressed together. Her head tilts down and a little to one side, eyes lowered, as if she's listening to someone shorter than she is. Rays of light pour out all around her. Under her feet is a dark crescent moon, held up by a small angel. Her mantle is blue-green and scattered with stars. This is the image on the tilma, the rough cloak of a man named Juan Diego, kept today in the basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City. You heard the story of the roses he carried in it back in year one. Today, just the picture, looked at slowly.
screen: `HANDS TOGETHER, EYES LOWERED.` → `LIGHT AROUND HER, MOON BENEATH.` → `TODAY, JUST THE PICTURE.`

segments.voice: First, the light and the moon. Catholic readers hear in this image a vision from the last book of the Bible. In the Douay-Rheims, John sees "a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet." The tilma looks like that line, painted. Second, her face. Her skin is dark, and her features are those of a native woman of that land, like Juan Diego himself, an Indigenous man. She doesn't look like a visitor from far away; she looks like the people who first gathered to see her. Third, the dark band tied above her belly. Some readers see in it the sign of a woman expecting a child. If they're right, the one the picture is really about is hidden: not on her arm, as in the icon from Poland, but within her. Elizabeth's greeting in Luke's Gospel says it: "blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Fourth, what she's doing. She stands in front of the sun, and she prays. Some readers say the picture spoke clearly to people who had honored the sun: here is a woman greater than the sun, and she bows her head to someone greater still. And yesterday's rule holds: no Catholic is required to believe the cloak is miraculous. Pilgrims come anyway, to look.

segments.voice: If you can, find a picture of the tilma; if not, let today's description stand in. Go slowly from the bottom up, one breath for each: the angel, the moon, the hem of her dress, her hands, her lowered eyes, then come back down to the band at her waist and stay there. If you pray, say the Hail Mary slowly and stop at the fruit of thy womb; if not, simply keep looking.
